what: Carpenter Technology melts and shapes specialty alloys: the nickel and titanium metals used in jet engine turbine blades, landing gear and medical implants, where ordinary steel would fail.
customers: Jet engine makers, aerospace suppliers, medical device companies and energy equipment makers.
money: premium alloys melted, forged and finished
powder metals, additive manufacturing materials and distribution
moat: Melting capacity for aerospace-qualified alloys is scarce, takes a decade and heavy capital to add, and every alloy is qualified into a specific engine part.
risks: Revenue depends on aircraft build rates, which Boeing and Airbus have repeatedly missed
Energy and medical demand are smaller and cannot offset an aerospace downturn
Melting is energy-intensive, so power costs move the margin
opportunities: Analysts see about 64% upside, with revenue up from $1.8B to $3.1B in four years
A 17.0% net margin, unusually high for a metals business, because capacity is tight
Engines already flying need replacement parts, an aftermarket that pays better than new builds
watch: Aerospace backlog and the price per pound realised on specialty alloys.
